passages.title: A Fresh Start at Work
passages.text:
When Tom started his new job, he felt **anxious** about meeting the team. His last manager had been **mean** with praise and even stingier with money, so the atmosphere in that office was often **unpleasant**. This time, though, the first week was **pleasant**. Colleagues smiled, invited him to lunch and shared useful tips about the company's systems. Hana, who sits next to him, is especially **easy to deal with**: she explains procedures patiently and never makes him feel stupid. They soon discovered that they had attended the same university, and as Hana likes to joke, **we’ve been mates ever since**.

The **current** project is a difficult one. The firm has lost customers to cheaper rivals, so the team must **develop an effective strategy** before the end of the quarter. Tom still feels nervous at meetings, but he admits that working with such friendly people has made the whole experience far less stressful than he expected.

passages.title: Exam Week Chaos
passages.text:
The week before the final exams was chaotic for Mai. On Monday morning she spilled her drink and groaned, “I **have got** coffee **on** my notes!” Then she discovered that her library card was about to **run out**, and her student visa would **expire** the following month, so she had to queue at two different offices. Because the exams were close, she tried to avoid wasting time, but with so many tasks she knew she would **be short on time** whenever she sat down to revise.

To protect her savings, she and her parents decided to **agree not to withdraw** any money from the account until the end of term. Her friends advised her to **engage in** group study, where students quiz one another and share summaries. “It is the only way to **get through** this period,” said Lan. Mai reluctantly agreed, and by Friday she felt calmer, even a little hopeful.

passages.title: Our Cosy New Flat
passages.text:
Our new flat is small but cosy. The living room has a **wooden floor** that we polish every month, and in the centre lies a thick **carpet** that keeps our feet warm in winter. Against the wall stands **a big soft sofa** where the whole family watches films, decorated with colourful **sofa cushions**. When guests stay, I put an extra **cushion** under their heads. The windows are covered with **blinds** that I lower in the afternoon to keep out the strong sun.

In the bathroom and the hallway, however, we chose practical **floor tiles**, because they are easy to wipe after muddy boots. One broken **tile** near the door still needs replacing, and the builder promised to fix it next week. In the bedroom, the warmest item is the **duvet**, which is so thick that I never need another blanket, even in January. Friends often say the flat feels like a hotel suite, which makes us proud.

passages.title: A Busy Family Home
passages.text:
Life in the Nguyen household is busy but well organised. The two brothers **share a bedroom**, so they have learned to keep their things tidy. Every evening the family likes to **have dinner in the dining room** instead of in front of the television, which gives them a chance to talk about their day. Their father often has to **work in the study** after the meal, preparing reports for the next morning.

Their mother, **a good cook**, buys fresh vegetables and meat at the weekend and stores them in **a fridge-freezer** that can hold a month of food. After supper she rinses the plates in the **kitchen sink**, while the older son helps by starting to **use the washing machine** to clean school uniforms for the following week. Neighbours often remark how calm the house feels, though the family admits that the schedule only works because everyone shares the chores.

passages.title: Saturday at the Shopping Centre
passages.text:
Last Saturday I took my **rucksack** and went to the new **shopping centre**, because everything I needed was **under one roof**: clothes, electronics, a pharmacy and even a cinema. The shops offered **a wide range of** products, and one clothing store had a special deal of **three for the price of two**. I could not resist, and I bought three shirts, although the **queue** at the till was so long that it took twenty minutes to pay.

At home I opened my wardrobe and realised that I **hardly ever wear** most of my old clothes. Looking at the pile, I understood that **half of it** was never worn at all. So I decided to **throw** some T-shirts **away** and keep only the ones I really like. My sister laughed and said that I always buy too much when there is a discount, and she may be right, but I still enjoyed the day out.

passages.title: A Day at the Cooking School
passages.text:
At the cooking school on Saturday, Chef Linh explained how the method can change flavour. First we learned to **boil** potatoes in a saucepan until they were soft, then to **fry** eggs in a frying pan with a little oil. After that, we practised how to **grill** sausages under a grill so that the fat dripped away. For the main course we chose **veal**, a tender meat from young cattle, and she showed us how to **roast** it in the oven with herbs and butter.

The next dish was **lamb**, which comes from young sheep and tastes richer than beef. Many students prefer fish, so we also cooked **mackerel**, an oily fish that is full of healthy fats. Finally, we learned to **bake** a loaf of bread in the oven without any oil. By evening, everyone had tasted six dishes, and I left with a notebook full of recipes.

passages.title: A Weekend Walk in the Country
passages.text:
Last weekend we took a long walk **on the banks of the river** that runs through our village. The path was **reasonably** flat, so even my grandmother could manage it without getting tired. We passed through some small **woods**, where the air smelled of pine and the birds were singing. The **scenery** was so beautiful that I stopped many times to take photographs.

**Apart from** a few cyclists, we met nobody on the way. Back in the village, we looked for somewhere to eat. The only café was **on the opposite side of the road** from the church, and to reach it we had to cross a quiet street and walk along the **pavement** for another fifty metres. The owner brought us hot soup and fresh bread, and we sat by the window watching the sun go down. It was a simple day, but one of the best we have had for months.

passages.title: A Close Call on the Road
passages.text:
Yesterday I happened to **see an accident** while waiting at the bus stop. My neighbour, who drives too fast, often says he will never **have an accident**, but I am not so sure after what I saw. A small white car **approached** the junction on **the main road** at high speed, just as a cyclist came out from a side street. The driver had to **brake hard**, but the car could not stop in time.

To miss the cyclist, he had to **swerve** to avoid him, and the car moved sharply to the left. Because of the sudden turn, it began to **crash into** **a parked car** that belonged to a local shopkeeper. The sound was terrifying, and people ran out of the shops to help. Fortunately, nobody was hurt badly. When the police arrived, they asked everyone to stay calm and to explain what they had seen. I realised how important it is to slow down near junctions.

passages.title: Road Safety in the News
passages.text:
A new report on road safety shows that careless driving continues to **injure** thousands of people every year. According to the authors, cyclists and pedestrians are more likely to **be injured** than car passengers, because they have no metal frame to protect them. Collisions also **damage** vehicles, street lamps and shop fronts, and the **damage to** public property costs local councils millions.

Young drivers, **in particular**, are at risk because they are less experienced and sometimes overconfident. The report also found that many people **have problems with** insurance after a crash, since the forms are long and the rules are hard to understand. The authors recommend lower speed limits near schools, better lighting and clearer advice for victims. A spokesperson for the transport ministry said that the government welcomes the findings and will study each proposal carefully before making any decision.

passages.title: Schools in England
passages.text:
In England, **state education** is paid for by the government and is free for every child. Most parents send their children to a **state school**, although some prefer a **private school**, which charges fees and **is operated by** a company, a charity or a religious group rather than by the local authority. Children usually **attend** a **nursery school** from the age of three, where they play and learn songs.

At five they move to **primary school**, and every **pupil** there studies reading, writing and basic maths with one main teacher. At eleven they join a **secondary school**, which is much larger and has a different teacher for each subject. Critics argue that private schools give wealthy families an unfair advantage, while supporters say they offer smaller classes and more activities. Whatever the type, every school must follow national safety rules, and inspectors visit regularly to check the standard of teaching in every classroom.

passages.title: After Sixteen: Choices for Young People
passages.text:
At the age of sixteen, British students must **take an exam** **in up to ten subjects**, and the results can shape their future. Some teenagers decide to **stay at school** for two more years to prepare for university. Others prefer **vocational training**, which teaches practical skills such as plumbing, cooking or computer repair. A third group wants to **get a job** immediately, hoping to earn money and gain experience.

My cousin Ben chose the college route. At first he found the workshops difficult and worried that he would never **make progress**, but his tutor encouraged him to practise every day. Within a few months he could repair a car engine alone. Ben says that choosing the right path matters more than following friends, and that nobody should feel forced to take the same road as everyone else. His mother agrees, and she is proud of how far he has come.

passages.title: Speaking Clearly in English
passages.text:
Learning to speak English well is a long journey. First, you need to **have a wide vocabulary**, because knowing many words helps you express your ideas. Second, you should speak **accurately**, which means using correct grammar and choosing the right word. As you practise, you will **become more fluent**, and one day you will talk **fluently**, without long pauses.

Pronunciation matters too. Learners who **have a good accent** are easier to understand, but nobody has to sound like a native speaker. It helps to study each **consonant** and **vowel** carefully, because English spelling does not always match the sounds. Learning the **alphabet** in phonetic symbols is a useful trick. The most important goal is to **make yourself understood**: if the listener grasps your message, you are communicating successfully. Try recording yourself every week, listen carefully, and ask a friend to give honest feedback on any sounds that seem difficult.

passages.title: How to Be a Good Language Learner
passages.text:
Every **language learner** wants to improve quickly, but success depends on attitude. First, you should **increase your vocabulary** by reading widely and noting new words. Second, **be willing to** speak even when you feel shy, because practice is the only way forward. You can also **experiment with** different methods, such as songs, films or flashcards, to find the one that suits you best.

Do not worry if you **get things wrong**; mistakes are a normal step. The secret is to **learn from your mistakes** and write each correction in a notebook. Some people **have a good ear for language**, hearing small differences between sounds, but anyone can improve with training. Young children often **pick things up** naturally, just by listening to adults, while adults usually need more study. When friends ask how you are doing, you can tell them how you **get on**: with patience and regular practice, most learners find that their confidence grows month by month, and speaking begins to feel less frightening.
